Love this question. Let me think freely here.

The BCG terms are academically clean but they're also kind of cold and hard to feel. Here are some analogy systems that I think could land better for an audience or in your project visuals:

🍳 The Kitchen Analogy

Centaur → The Chef with a Sous Chef. You decide the dish, the flavors, the vision. The sous chef chops, preps, executes the technical bits. You stay the author of the meal.

Cyborg → Cooking together in real time — you and the sous chef are trading the spoon back and forth, both learning from each other mid-dish. The recipe is being invented as you go.

Self-Automator → You ordered Uber Eats. Food arrives. You ate. You have no idea what was in it, and you definitely didn't cook.

🚗 The Driving Analogy

Centaur → You drive, GPS gives turn-by-turn. You could get there without it, but it's faster. You're still driving.

Cyborg → You and the GPS are learning a new city together — you're making judgment calls, it's giving live data, you're both adapting.

Self-Automator → Full self-driving. You're in the back seat. You've forgotten how to drive. You don't even know which city you're in.

🎸 The Band Analogy

Centaur → You're the songwriter, AI is the session musician. You wrote the song, they play it better than you could.

Cyborg → You're co-writing with a collaborator in the studio. The song is genuinely co-authored. You're both changed by it.

Self-Automator → You asked AI to write, record, and release a song. You put your name on it. You can't play a single chord.

Beyond the 3 archetypes — other signals of AI style

Here's where it gets more interesting for your project. There are behaviors that reveal the style without labeling it:

Behavioral tells a tool could catch:

Do you ever disagree with what AI gives you? (Centaur/Cyborg do. Self-Automator rarely does.)

Do you paste the whole task in one go, or do you shape it across turns?

Do you edit AI output, or post it as-is?

When AI gives you something wrong — do you know it's wrong?

That last one is the sharpest signal. The Self-Automator can't catch the AI's mistakes — because they've already offloaded the judgment needed to evaluate the output. That's the cliff edge.

A framing I find really punchy for your thesis context:

Centaur: you're the jockey.
Cyborg: you're fused with the horse.
Self-Automator: the horse left without you.

What's the context you're thinking about this for — is it for a presentation slide, or for the Agency Timeline labels, or something else?

OK this is a genuinely fun and rich design problem. Let me think wide first, then build something.

Here's the full possibility space I'm seeing — before narrowing:

The core challenge: After a prompt/response pair, show the user what mode they just used AI in, in a way that's delightful and instantly understood.

Category 1: Persistent ambient indicators (always visible, low-friction)

A tiny steering wheel icon next to each exchange — full wheel = you're driving (Centaur), half-faded wheel = shared (Cyborg), ghosted wheel = backseat (Self-Automator)

A "lane" on the left sidebar that shifts color temperature as the conversation progresses — warm human-colored to cool AI-colored

A live "grip meter" — literal hands gripping a wheel, loosening visually per exchange

Category 2: Post-exchange micro-animations (your driving analogy, expanded)

The car scene you described — a tiny animated car plays for 2-3 seconds after each AI response, showing who's doing what

Or: a mini film strip on the side that accumulates — each exchange is one frame in the strip

Category 3: Metaphor-per-session systems (adaptive, assigned at session start based on early exchanges)

Session gets classified as one of 5-6 metaphor "skins": driving, cooking, music, climbing, dancing

The same 3-mode idea plays out in the metaphor's language

"You're the chef, AI is the knife" vs "AI is cooking for you"

Category 4: Score that isn't a score (no numbers, but position on a spectrum)

A tug-of-war rope visualization — per exchange, the knot shifts left or right

A spotlight that moves across a stage: you center, AI center, or AI alone in the light

Category 5: Honest/funny self-aware labels

After each exchange: "You drove this one" / "You co-piloted" / "You were a passenger"

With a little emoji glyph, no explanation needed

Now, your specific car idea is the strongest visually. Let me build it as an interactive demo — one where you can click through all three modes and see the animation:

[Interactive Widget: ai_mode_car_animation]

That's the core car metaphor as an interactive demo. Now let me lay out all the other directions so you can pick:

Other directions worth exploring:

The Grip Meter — a single image per exchange: two hands on a steering wheel, where hand opacity represents how much control you held. Full hands = Centaur, one fading hand = Cyborg, ghosted hands = Self-Automator. Extremely minimal, could live as a tiny badge.

The Film Frame strip — each prompt/response pair adds one thumbnail frame to a horizontal filmstrip on the left sidebar. Frame tint color = your mode that exchange. Over time you see your session's "color rhythm" — did you drift toward the backseat?

The Kitchen version — you as chef with a sous-chef. Could be funnier and more universally relatable than driving. "You plated this." vs "You two cooked together." vs "You ordered delivery."

The Muscle metaphor — most brutally honest. Each exchange either shows a flexed arm (you did the thinking) or an atrophying one (you didn't use that muscle). More confrontational — probably strongest for your thesis argument specifically.

The "receipt" after a session — not per-exchange, but at session end: a receipt-style breakdown. "3 exchanges: you drove 2, AI drove 1." Fast, legible, no animation needed.

Which direction feels closest to what you want to build for the actual project? And — is this a live overlay on a real chat interface, or a standalone visualization that receives a chat export?

OK this is the exact right design problem. Let me think through this precisely before building.

The minimap panel needs to do two things per exchange:

Show who drove this exchange (Centaur / Cyborg / Self-Automator flavor)

Show how much AI influence leaked into the next turn (indirect influence — the invisible thing)

Each prompt+response = one small row/unit in the minimap. As exchanges stack, the minimap becomes a session history you can glance at and see your pattern.

The visual language I want to try: each exchange is a horizontal bar — split into human-colored left side and AI-colored right side. The split ratio = who shaped this exchange. Below/above it, a thin thread shows indirect influence bleeding into the next one. Small, compact, readable at minimap scale.

Let me build this as a right-panel mockup:

[Interactive Widget: agency_minimap_panel]

Hover over any bar in the minimap to see the tooltip. Click "Send" to load more exchanges.

Here's the design logic I made explicit in this:

Per exchange unit (the horizontal bar):

Blue left = how much you shaped this exchange

Purple right = how much AI shaped it

The ratio is the primary signal — glanceable in under a second

The mode name badge sits on the right so you can read it without hovering

The indirect influence thread (the dots between bars):

This is the invisible thing — AI's answer to exchange 2 subtly shaped what you asked in exchange 3

The dots + label surface that connection without being accusatory

They only appear when influence actually bled across turns

Session bar (top of panel):

Running average of the whole session

Updates live as exchanges accumulate

Gives you the "overall posture" of the conversation at a glance

What still needs to be designed:

The big open question is: who classifies each exchange? In your project, is this a manual thing the user labels themselves (which is your original thesis move — the act of marking is the competence-preserving act), or is it an automatic LLM analysis running in the background?

That choice completely changes what the panel means and how honest it can be.

Got it. The key insight you're pointing at: the bottom bar is where the user lives — it's where their next action happens — so that's the most natural place to show them who they currently are, not buried in the side panel.

Let me design this as a full chat interface mockup — minimap on the right, but the bottom prompt bar has the live identity indicator that shifts as the session progresses:

[Interactive Widget: agency_chat_interface_with_meter]

Hit Send a few times to walk through the exchanges and watch everything shift together.

Here's the design logic behind the bottom bar specifically:

The three elements in the identity bar work as a system:

The tiny car scene is the story — who's in what position, updating per exchange. The mode pill is the label — the word for it, color-coded. The grip meter is the number — how much of this conversation has been yours, as a single bar.

All three change together on every exchange, so even without reading anything the user gets a visual sense of drift. If the bar keeps shrinking and the pill turns orange, that's felt before it's understood.

Why the bottom bar is the right place:

It's the moment just before the user types. That's exactly when they can do something about it. Showing the identity at the top of the screen is information. Showing it right above the input is a gentle mirror — "here's who you've been, now what do you want to do?"

The open design question for you:

Right now the grip meter shows "your grip" per exchange. But you could make it show the session average instead — which would shift more slowly and tell a different story. Per-exchange feels reactive, session average feels like a posture. Which one is more honest for your thesis argument?
